title: My day
verifiedBy: Claude Opus 5 — LLM review, authorised by repo owner

rules.text: The -yo ending picks its shape from the last vowel of the stem: a stem with a or o in it takes -ayo, everything else takes -eoyo, and a verb built on haeyo simply becomes haeyo. Written in Latin letters the choice is visible on the page — meogeoyo, masyeoyo, jayo — which is one real advantage of learning this course's spelling.

One Korean present does the work of both English presents. bap-eul meogeoyo is 'I eat' and 'I am eating' alike, and nothing in the sentence chooses between them. Korean does have a way of saying that something is going on right now; it is a later level's, and reaching for it here is unnecessary.

Leave the subject out whenever the situation supplies it. Achim-e bap-eul meogeoyo is a complete sentence about yourself. Putting jeo-neun in front of every sentence is grammatical and it is the clearest sign of an English speaker — it reads as 'as for ME', as if somebody else were being compared.
-e marks a point in time and goes on the time word: achim-e, jeonyeok-e, bam-e. It is not a word of its own and it never stands alone.

Some time words take NO marker at all: oneul, maeil, eoje, naeil. There is no -e on any of them, ever. They can take the topic marker if you want to set that day apart — oneul-eun — but never the point-in-time one.
A noun plus haeyo makes a verb, and Korean makes hundreds of them this way: gongbu ('study') plus haeyo gives gongbuhaeyo, il ('work') gives ilhaeyo. Learn the noun and you have most of the verb.

Negating one of those verbs SPLITS it: gongbu an haeyo, never an gongbuhaeyo. The an goes in front of haeyo, which means it lands in the middle of what looked like a single word. This is the one place where the two halves have to be written apart.

Time words come early — before the object, usually right after the subject if there is one. Maeil achim-e keopi-reul masyeoyo puts the when first, the what second and the verb last, which is the ordinary shape of a Korean sentence about a habit.
The verb never changes for the person. meogeoyo is 'I eat', 'you eat', 'he eats' and 'they eat' — there is no ending to add for a third person and nothing to agree with.

sentences.cue: I get up in the morning.

words.note: 'I', from M1, and in this module it is mostly absent: a habit you are describing about yourself needs no subject once the conversation is about you.
'Morning', and also 'breakfast' — the meal is named after the time of day, so achim-e bap-eul meogeoyo is what you say for having breakfast.
The point-in-time marker: achim-e 'in the morning', jeonyeok-e 'in the evening'. It attaches to the time word and says when. Later it marks a place — the same job: a point, in time or in space.
'Get up, rise'. The stem is ireona-, which already ends in the a that the ending wants, so the two merge and nothing is added — ireonayo, not ireona-ayo.

sentences.trap: English says 'in the morning' with a word in front. Korean marks the time word behind, and there is nothing corresponding to 'in' standing on its own — looking for one will only produce a word that does not belong.
sentences.sound: juh-nun A-chim-e i-ruh-NA-yo. The m of achim runs into the -e, so it is heard as a-chi-me. ireonayo has four light beats; the r in it is a soft tap, closer to the middle of English 'better' than to an English r.

sentences.glossEn: I eat a meal in the morning.

words.note: 'Morning', and also 'breakfast' — the meal is named after the time of day, so achim-e bap-eul meogeoyo is what you say for having breakfast.
The point-in-time marker: achim-e 'in the morning', jeonyeok-e 'in the evening'. It attaches to the time word and says when. Later it marks a place — the same job: a point, in time or in space.
'A meal', from M3 — with achim-e in front of it, the morning one.
'Eat', from M3, now in its plain -yo shape. The stem meok- ends in a consonant and the vowel in it is neither a nor o, so the ending is -eoyo.

sentences.trap: There is no word here for 'breakfast'. Korean names the meal by the time of day it happens, so 'morning meal' is the whole of it — and a learner hunting for a separate breakfast word is hunting for something the language does without.
sentences.sound: A-chi-me BA-bul MUH-guh-yo. Two liaisons in a row: achim runs into -e and bap runs into -eul, so the middle of the sentence flows as a-chi-me ba-bul. That linking is automatic and is what makes Korean sound smooth rather than clipped.

variations.changed: the evening meal, by the same logic

variations.cue: I drink coffee in the morning.
variations.changed: a different habit at the same hour
the negative, with an in front of the verb

mistake.why: Without -e, achim is not a time any more — the two nouns sit together and it reads as 'morning-meal' as a thing rather than as when you eat. The marker is what turns a noun into a time.

sentences.mnemonic: Korean eats the morning, not breakfast.

words.note: 'I', from M1, and in this module it is mostly absent: a habit you are describing about yourself needs no subject once the conversation is about you.
'Every day'. It takes NO marker — it is one of the time words that stand bare, and putting -e on it is the commonest early mistake.
'Study', noun and verb written as one word, as it is said when nothing separates them. Apart — gongbu haeyo — means the same, and is what you write once a negative slips between.

sentences.trap: maeil takes no marker. Every other time word in this module wears -e, and this one does not — there is no rule you can hear, so it is learned as a small list.
sentences.sound: juh-nun MAE-il gong-boo-HAE-yo. maeil is two beats, mae and il, not one. gongbuhaeyo is four, and the whole thing is said evenly with no stressed syllable anywhere.

mistake.why: -e has been put on maeil, by analogy with achim-e. It does not take one, and there is no version of this sentence in which it does.

sentences.mnemonic: Some time words wear the marker; maeil never does.

sentences.glossEn: As for today, I am working.

words.note: 'Today', and like maeil it takes no -e. It can take the topic marker, oneul-eun, and then it means 'as for today' — setting today apart from other days.
'Work', built the same way as gongbuhaeyo: the noun il ('work') plus haeyo. Same pattern, same behaviour, including what happens to it in a negative.

sentences.trap: The topic marker on a time word sets that day apart — 'today, as opposed to other days'. It is not the same as the -e marker, and it is not decoration: it is why this sentence implies a contrast that plain oneul ilhaeyo would not.
sentences.sound: o-neu-run IL-hae-yo. The l of oneul links into the -eun, so it is heard as o-neu-run. ilhaeyo's h softens almost to nothing between the l and the vowel, so many speakers say i-rae-yo at speed.

variations.changed: a different verb under the same contrast
without the topic marker — a plain statement, with no sense of comparing days
the negative, and the contrast is now the point of the sentence

mistake.why: The point-in-time marker has been used on a word that refuses it. oneul stands bare, or takes the topic marker; -e is not available to it.

sentences.usage: Saying what today in particular holds.
sentences.mnemonic: -eun on a day means: this day, unlike the others.

words.note: 'I', from M1, and in this module it is mostly absent: a habit you are describing about yourself needs no subject once the conversation is about you.
'Korean', the language, from M1 — the thing being learned, so it takes -eul.
'Every day'. It takes NO marker — it is one of the time words that stand bare, and putting -e on it is the commonest early mistake.
'Learn', from M3. The stem baeu- ends in u, and u plus the ending contract into -wo, giving baewoyo. Every one of these contractions is the same rule making the word easier to say.

sentences.trap: The time word has slipped in behind the object here rather than in front of it. Korean lets it sit either side, because the markers say what each word is doing — the one place nothing may move is the verb, which stays last.
sentences.sound: juh-nun han-GOONG-ma-rul MAE-il BAE-wuh-yo. baewoyo is the stem baeu- with the ending pulled onto it, which is why the u turns into a w sound. Three beats, evenly said.

variations.changed: the time word moved in front of the object — the sentence means exactly the same thing
subject and time dropped, down to the bare habit
a different learner, an unchanged verb

mistake.why: The time word has been put after the verb, where English happily puts it. Nothing may follow the verb in a Korean sentence — that is the one fixed rule of the word order.

sentences.usage: Describing a routine that includes a study habit.
sentences.mnemonic: Move anything you like in front of the verb; move nothing behind it.

sentences.cue: I drink tea in the evening.

words.note: 'Evening', and the evening meal, as achim covers morning and breakfast. The final k softens to g when -e follows, but the word is jeonyeok and that is how it is written here.
The point-in-time marker: achim-e 'in the morning', jeonyeok-e 'in the evening'. It attaches to the time word and says when. Later it marks a place — the same job: a point, in time or in space.
'Tea', from M1, as the thing drunk.
'Drink', from M3. The stem masi- ends in i, and i plus the -eoyo ending contract into -yeoyo, which is why the word comes out as masyeoyo rather than masieoyo.

sentences.trap: masyeoyo does not look like the stem it comes from. The stem is masi-, and the i has merged with the ending — so a learner looking for masi inside the word will find only the sh sound it turned into.
sentences.sound: juh-NYUH-ge CHA-rul ma-SHUH-yo. The k of jeonyeok softens to a g in front of the -e, so it is heard as juh-nyuh-ge. The word is still jeonyeok, which is why it is spelled that way here and the softening is described rather than written.

mistake.why: Without -e the time word has become part of the thing drunk — 'evening tea' as a kind of tea. The marker is what makes it a time.

sentences.mnemonic: No marker, no time — just two nouns next to each other.

words.note: 'Night' — the dark part, after jeonyeok. There is another word spelled the same way meaning 'chestnut'; it is not taught in this course, so bam here is always the night.
The point-in-time marker: achim-e 'in the morning', jeonyeok-e 'in the evening'. It attaches to the time word and says when. Later it marks a place — the same job: a point, in time or in space.
'Sleep'. The stem is ja-, and because it already ends in a, the ending's own a disappears into it: there is no ja-ayo, only jayo. Short verbs are where that merging is easiest to see.

sentences.trap: Two words is a whole sentence. There is no subject and none is missing, and an English speaker will feel the gap where 'I' should be — that feeling is the thing to get over.
sentences.sound: BA-me JA-yo. The stem of jayo is ja-, and because it already ends in a, the ending's own a disappears into it: there is no ja-ayo, only jayo. That merging happens with every stem ending in the same vowel as its ending.

sentences.mnemonic: Two words, one whole sentence, and nothing missing.

sentences.sound: MIN-soo-nun MAE-il IL-hae-yo. Every syllable is even. English wants to lean on the first syllable of Minsu and the language does not lean anywhere.

words.note: 'I', from M1, and in this module it is mostly absent: a habit you are describing about yourself needs no subject once the conversation is about you.
'Today', and like maeil it takes no -e. It can take the topic marker, oneul-eun, and then it means 'as for today' — setting today apart from other days.
'Study' as a NOUN — the activity. Put haeyo behind it and you have the verb: gongbuhaeyo. Korean builds dozens of verbs this way, so the noun is half a verb you can make.
'Not', in front of the verb, from M3. With a noun-built verb like gongbuhaeyo it wedges INTO the word: gongbu an haeyo. Not a variant — the only way to negate this kind of verb.
'Do' — the most useful verb in the language, because it turns a noun into a verb: gongbu haeyo, il haeyo. One word when nothing comes between, two when something does, as in a negative.

sentences.trap: You cannot put an in front of gongbuhaeyo. The verb is a noun with haeyo behind it, and the negative goes between them — which means the word you learned as one piece has to be written as two the moment you negate it.
sentences.sound: juh-nun O-neul GONG-boo an HAE-yo. There is a small break after gongbu, and an leans onto haeyo so the last two words come out almost as one: an-hae-yo. That grouping is the audible proof that an belongs to the verb, not to the noun.
